### Two Measles Deaths Bring New Attention to Vaccination and Outbreak Prevention


Pennsylvania health officials have confirmed two measles associated deaths in Lancaster County, marking the first measles related deaths in the state in 35 years. Both individuals were unvaccinated, according to the Pennsylvania Department of Health.


The announcement comes as measles activity continues to affect communities across Pennsylvania and other parts of the United States. State health officials have confirmed 393 measles cases across 28 Pennsylvania counties during 2026. The developments are renewing attention on vaccination, early detection and the importance of preventing the spread of a disease that was once largely eliminated in the United States.


The Pennsylvania Department of Health said the two deaths occurred among Lancaster County residents. Officials have not released additional identifying information, citing privacy concerns for the individuals and their families.


## Why the Pennsylvania Measles Outbreak Matters


Measles is among the most contagious infectious diseases. It spreads through the air when an infected person breathes, coughs or sneezes. The virus can remain infectious in an indoor space for as long as two hours after an infected person has left, according to Pennsylvania health officials.


The disease often begins with symptoms that can resemble other respiratory infections. Fever, cough, a runny nose and red or watery eyes may appear first. A characteristic rash generally develops several days later, beginning on the head and moving downward across the body.


Symptoms can develop between seven and 21 days after exposure. Because a person can spread measles before the rash appears, identifying possible exposure early is important for limiting transmission.


Although many people recover from measles, the illness can sometimes become severe. Complications can include pneumonia and encephalitis, which is inflammation of the brain. Pennsylvania health authorities say almost 20 percent of people who contract measles may require hospitalization. Deaths are uncommon, but they can occur.


## Vaccination Remains the Main Protection


The latest deaths have also placed renewed focus on the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine, commonly known as the MMR vaccine.


Pennsylvania health officials say two doses provide the strongest protection against measles, with the department describing the vaccine as providing 97 percent lifetime protection after two doses.


The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention also provides current MMR recommendations for different age groups and circumstances. Vaccination schedules can vary depending on age, previous vaccination, travel plans and other factors, so people who are uncertain about their status should speak with a qualified healthcare professional.


Vaccination does more than protect an individual. High vaccination coverage also helps reduce opportunities for the virus to spread through schools, workplaces and communities. This is particularly important for people who cannot receive certain vaccines or who may face greater health risks from infection.


## Lancaster County at the Centre of the Outbreak


Lancaster County has been a major focus of Pennsylvania's measles response. The state has reported nearly half of its confirmed 2026 cases in southern Lancaster County, according to health officials.


The state has responded by expanding vaccination access and public health outreach. More than 4,100 MMR vaccinations have been administered through pop up clinics in affected areas since the outbreak began in April. Pennsylvania officials have also announced plans for additional clinics in the coming weeks.


The response demonstrates how vaccination campaigns can be used alongside disease monitoring and public education when outbreaks occur. Health departments can identify potential exposures, advise people who may have been exposed and provide vaccination opportunities for those who need protection.


## What People Should Know About Measles Symptoms


Recognising possible symptoms is important, particularly for people who have recently been exposed to someone with measles or who are not fully vaccinated.


Common symptoms include:


- High fever
- Cough
- Runny nose
- Red or watery eyes
- A widespread rash


Anyone who believes they may have been exposed and develops symptoms should contact a healthcare provider before visiting a medical facility in person. Calling ahead allows healthcare workers to take precautions that can reduce the risk of exposing other patients and staff.


People who have questions about a possible exposure can also contact their local or state health department for guidance.


## Prevention Is Especially Important for Vulnerable Groups


Measles can pose a particular risk to young children and other people who are more vulnerable to serious complications. Pennsylvania's Department of Health notes that children younger than five can face significant health risks from measles.


Protecting vulnerable people is one reason public health officials encourage eligible people to remain up to date with recommended vaccinations. When fewer people are protected, an infectious disease can find more opportunities to spread.


The current Pennsylvania outbreak also shows why communities should not assume that a disease is no longer a threat simply because it has been uncommon for many years. When vaccination coverage declines or immunity gaps develop, diseases that once appeared distant can return.


## A Reminder to Check Vaccination Records


For families, one practical step is to check vaccination records and discuss any uncertainty with a healthcare professional.


Adults who are unsure whether they received the recommended doses may also benefit from speaking with their healthcare provider, particularly before international travel or when entering settings where exposure to measles is possible.


Pennsylvania health officials have stressed that vaccination is the best available protection against measles. The state is also working with healthcare providers and schools to improve awareness and preparedness as cases continue to be monitored.


The two deaths in Lancaster County are a serious reminder that measles is not simply a disease of the past. Strong vaccination coverage, rapid public health responses and reliable medical information remain essential tools for limiting outbreaks and protecting communities.
